findings.finding: Planned takeaway says 'treat the figure as a ceiling' and the brief frames the notice number as a cap. Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3(d)-(e) says the notice shows proposed taxes only and excludes special assessments, voter-approved levies after certification (bond and school referenda), levy-limit increases, disaster and tort-judgment amounts and contamination tax; subd. 3(d) notes a pending referendum 'may be higher than shown'. CBS Minnesota (Hilgart/McCarthy): the final bill 'could be more or it could be less'. Only the TAXING AUTHORITY levy is capped (DOR), not a homeowner's final bill; valuation, classification and credits also move it.
findings.fix: Rewrite the A3 takeaway, answer sentence and REQ-3 acceptance as: the notice is a proposal; each authority's final levy is generally capped at its proposed levy (DOR) but your bill can still differ because of items the notice excludes and your own valuation/classification; compare current vs proposed by authority, attend the hearing of the body driving the change. Put the exclusions list (subd. 3(e)) and 'could be more or less' in the first answer, FAQ and takeaway. Never write 'ceiling' for the parcel figure.

findings.finding: 'What the Hearing Cannot Change: final levy cannot exceed proposed; town and state general tax proposed equals final' omits statutory limits. Subd. 6(a)(1)-(9) lets city, county, school, metro and regional-library levies exceed the proposed levy for post-certification voter approvals, disaster/tort amounts approved under subd. 6a, levy-limit increases, emergency debt and unallotment; subd. 6(b) says the cap does not apply to towns and special districts other than regional library and metropolitan districts; subd. 3(d) says a town's final tax equals proposed unless it changes its levy at a special town meeting.
findings.fix: Attribute 'can be set lower, not higher' to the Minnesota DOR press release (2026-11-12), add 'with limited statutory exceptions' and name the main exceptions from subd. 6(a); state the town and state general tax rule with its special-town-meeting exception; keep Dec 28, 2026 as DOR's stated date.

findings.finding: Readiness and exclusions treat hearing timing as wholly unverified. Subd. 3(c) is a verified primary source: the meeting must occur after November 24 and not before 6:00 p.m., the notice must list time/place and a contact website/phone; DOR says meetings run late November to late December and are required for cities over 500, counties, school districts, regional library authorities, metropolitan taxing districts.
findings.fix: Optional: WRITE may state 'after November 24, not before 6:00 p.m.' attributed to Minn. Stat. 275.065 subd. 3(c) and tell readers to use the date/time printed on their own notice. Keep specific start times for any given body, and the valuation-appeal path, excluded.

findings.finding: Section 1 as briefed carries only the Treasury 'plan years beginning after December 31, 2027' date. The statute (Pub. L. 117-328 sec. 101(c) via 26 USC 414A note) says plan years beginning after December 31, 2024. The gap is not resolved by any saved source; good-faith interim compliance is not verified.
findings.fix: Section 1, FAQ and takeaway state both dates with attribution (Treasury SB-0690 for the final regulations; the statute for the enactment date), say the sources do not tell a worker which date governs a given plan, and never say or imply a current plan is exempt or has until 2028. Do not print 'TD 10061' or any Federal Register number.

findings.finding: Planned table 'default rate by year: 3% to 10% in seven steps' reads as what plans will do. Statute allows a first-year default of 3% to 10% and increases of 1 point 'to at least 10 percent, but not more than 15 percent'; Treasury says final regulations give employers flexibility in timing and amount of increases within statutory limits and the first increase follows an initial participation period.
findings.fix: Label the table 'minimum path under the rule, our illustrative arithmetic': start 3, +1 per completed year of participation, 10 after seven steps, plan may start higher (up to 10) or step faster up to 15. Worked example ($60,000: $1,800 at 3%, $6,000 at 10%) must say pre-tax salary-only arithmetic, not a prediction.

findings.finding: Exemptions are paraphrased loosely. 414A(c)(4)(B): small business exception ends 1 year after the close of the first taxable year in which the employer normally employed MORE than 10 employees (not simply '10 or fewer'); (c)(4)(A) employer in existence less than 3 years; (c)(2) pre-enactment plans (before Dec 29, 2022) but not an employer adopting a multiple-employer plan afterward (c)(2)(B); (c)(1) SIMPLE; (c)(3) governmental and church. Treasury says the final regulations 'clarify' these, and the detail of that clarification was not read.
findings.fix: State exemptions at statute precision, attribute detail changes to the regulations only as 'Treasury says the final rules clarify them', do not describe regulation-level definitions. Takeaway: check whether the plan is exempt or voluntarily auto-enrolls with another default.

findings.finding: Brief labels the schedule/example 'our internal arithmetic' (calculated). _decision-evidence/_mindmap-execution reject trivial arithmetic as an originality claim, and a calculated basis needs an executed packet (code, inputs, output hashes, replay).

Either way, the page's main answer rests on Treasury/IRC, not on our arithmetic.

findings.finding: Takeaway 'reversal is Chase's discretion unless the problem is an electronic fund transfer error under Reg E' and the Zelle section risk implying an outage-delayed Zelle payment or an outage fee is a Reg E error. 12 CFR 1005.11(a)(1) lists specific error types (unauthorized, incorrect, omitted, computational, wrong amount from terminal, undocumented, documentation request); no saved source says a delay or an overdraft fee caused by an outage qualifies, and source silence is not proof either way.
findings.fix: State Reg E only as: if you believe an electronic transfer was unauthorized, incorrect or omitted, notice of error within 60 days of the statement and the 10-business-day / 45-day investigation clock apply (cite 1005.11). Say plainly that sources checked do not say whether outage-related fees or delays count as errors; keep the fee-reversal ask as a request to Chase. Quote Zelle's statement directly ('An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments').
